title: AIAD (AI-Aided Design)
pitch: Computer-aided design is evolving. Agents can now review CAD/BIM designs with you: query, isolate, cut, annotate. And they see your viewport, so "what do we know about this door?" just works.
about_excerpt: Computer-aided design is evolving. Agents can now review CAD/BIM designs with you: query, isolate, cut, annotate. And they see your viewport, so "what do we know about this door?" just works. Like 1 Comment Story Updates From Computer-Aided Design to AI-Aided Design Inspiration CAD has been computer -aided for fifty years, and the computer's role hasn't changed much. Every question about a design still gets answered by a human clicking through it, and every problem found that way gets typed into a form somewhere away from the model. I've spent years building the browser viewer that does the clicking-through. WebMCP made me wonder what happens when the viewer stops being a display and becomes a set of tools an agent can use. Not AI that generates a design, but AI that can review one. What it does A BIM design review app: a Revit model in the Autodesk Platform Services Viewer, with the viewer and the review's issue list exposed to an agent as WebMCP tools. You walk the building in first person, select something, and talk. The agent searches design metadata, browses the model hierarchy, isolates and frames parts, colors objects by any property, etc. Then it drafts an issue against it, revises the draft while you watch, and submits when you say so. show-issue puts you back inside the model at the reporter's eye position, with the viewer state they had. It reads the current selection and camera every turn, so "what is this door?" resolves without either of us naming anything. How I built it APS Viewer loads and renders the translated Revit model, and provides the first-person walkthrough. WebMCP registers several tools straight from the page, with return values shaped for a token budget rather than for a database client. The form is the draft. draft-issue writes into the same form you can type into. submit-issue takes no arguments at all. The only thing that can be filed is what's on screen. Tools register conditionally on viewer state : none until geometry has loaded, and all ten dropped before a different design loads. A property query against a half-loaded model doesn't give you a degraded answer, it gives you a confident wrong one. Nothing leaves the browser. Issues go to IndexedDB. "The north stair doesn't meet code" next to a client's project name is a professional judgement about someone else's building, and a hackathon demo has no user auth to protect it with. What I learned The interesting work wasn't wiring up tools, it was deciding what a tool should say back. A property query on a real model returns thousands of rows, which is useless to an agent. Returning counts, outliers and a category breakdown is what turns guessing into answering. My favourite question in the demo, "how many doors have no fire rating set?", is one no amount of looking at the screen can answer, and it costs about twenty tokens. The best tool I wrote was the one I deleted. I built a screenshot tool so the agent could check its own camera moves. It worked, and then I confirmed the host reads the viewport directly without being asked. A viewpoint beats a picture anyway. Half the problems worth reporting are only visible because a floor was isolated or the model was cut at mid-height. Store the camera alone and the reviewer arrives at the right coordinates staring at an opaque wall, which is worse than not navigating at all, because it makes the issue look wrong. Challenges Shared state. Two actors driving one camera needs a clear owner. Every agent move is an animated flight rather than a cut, because a cut drops you somewhere else in the building with nothing to say how the two places relate. Trust. If submit-issue accepted overrides, the review step would be a formality. The agent says "I set it to high and submitted it" and you have no way to check. Forcing every edit back through the on-screen form is what makes "looks good, submit" mean something. Scale. Engineering models have hundreds of thousands of objects. Every list is capped and carries its true total, and color-coding paints recursively, so 5,000 doors cost one id. Deixis. Making "this" work meant treating the viewport as context the agent always has, rather than something it asks about. video_transcript_excerpt: All right, let's take a quick look at this BIM model. Show me all the rooms color-coded by type. >> Got it. Let me take a look. I'll set the model style showing just the rooms color-coded by type. >> Awesome. Thank you. That looks good. Are all the rooms labeled properly? >> Sure, I'll check the labels. Not quite. Room 224 is misspelled cafeteria and room 101 is abbreviated vest, which might be intentional. >> Hmm, the typo is a good catch. Please create a low severity issue for the QA with due date by the end of next week. >> Sure, I'll take care of that. Done. The low severity issue for the room 224 typo is drafted, assigned to Yuki, and due Sunday, September 13th. Want me to submit it? >> No, that's okay. Let me take a look and I'll submit it myself. >> Sounds good. Give it a quick review and let me know if you want any tweaks before you send it. >> Awesome. This looks good. Now, uh I want to check out the cafeteria. Please take me inside the cafeteria room. >> Okay, I'll take a look. You're now inside the cafeteria looking across the room. >> Mhm. What information do we have about this door? >> Let me check that. It's a curtain wall double glass door on the entry level about 1.83 m wide by 2.13 m high. The mark is 101. >> Is there any fire rating on this door? >> I'll check that. Nope. The fire rating field is there, but it's blank. So, no rating is specified. >> Oh, okay. That's a problem. Um, please draft a high severity issue for the architect and this must be solved by the end of this month. >> All right, I'll draft that. Done. The high severity code compliance issue is drafted for Marta, due September 30th with the door and current view attached. >> Perfect. Thank you. >> You're welcome.

live_observation.first_impression: The URL opens Autodesk Platform Services Viewer v7 developer documentation, not a BIM review demo.
live_observation.action_attempted: Inspected the documentation landing page for the claimed CAD/BIM workflow.
live_observation.after_state: Documentation navigation showed viewer, model-property, and viewer-state topics; no loaded design or review controls appeared.
live_observation.notes: The supplied demo URL is a generic Autodesk developer guide rather than the claimed AIAD application.
